concepts.name: Legislative Basis and Parent Act of Wetlands Rules 2017
key_dimensions: Enacted under Section 25 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 — not a standalone legislation
Supersedes the earlier Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2010 — key differences and why 2010 rules were criticized
Relationship with other environmental laws: Wildlife Protection Act, Forest Conservation Act, Ramsar Convention obligations
UPSC trap: Confusing it with a standalone Act vs. subordinate legislation under EPA 1986

concepts.name: Definition of 'Wetland' under the 2017 Rules
key_dimensions: Specific legal definition: areas of marsh, fen, peatland, natural or artificial, permanent or temporary, with water that is static or flowing, fresh, brackish or salt
Includes mangroves and coral reefs but excludes paddy fields — a critical UPSC trap
Comparison with Ramsar Convention's broader definition of wetlands (Article 1.1)
Exclusion of river channels, except in estuarine areas — boundary ambiguity and litigation potential

concepts.name: Wetlands Authority: State-Level Structure and Composition
key_dimensions: 2017 Rules shift authority from Central Wetlands Regulatory Authority (under 2010 Rules) to State-level Wetlands Authorities — decentralization angle
Composition: Chief Minister as Chairperson (UPSC trap: not the Chief Secretary or Environment Minister)
Includes representation from local bodies and community — participatory governance dimension
Contrast with 2010 Rules which had a Central Authority — federal vs. centralized governance debate

concepts.name: Abolition of Central Wetlands Regulatory Authority (CWRA)
key_dimensions: CWRA established under 2010 Rules was dissolved by the 2017 Rules — no equivalent central body now
Functions transferred to State Wetlands Authorities and MoEFCC at central level
Criticism: weakening of central oversight and uniform national standards
UPSC trap: Questions asking which body currently regulates wetlands at national level — MoEFCC retains advisory/coordinating role

concepts.name: Prohibited Activities in Wetlands under 2017 Rules
key_dimensions: Specific prohibitions: reclamation, solid waste dumping, discharge of untreated effluents, encroachment
UPSC trap: Prohibited activities are listed in the Rules, not left to State discretion — central mandate
Comparison with 2010 Rules which had a broader and more stringent prohibited activities list
Interplay with EIA Notification 2006 for projects near wetlands

concepts.name: Regulated (Permissible) Activities in Wetlands
key_dimensions: Activities that require State Wetlands Authority permission: certain infrastructure, tourism, research
Key shift from 2010 Rules: 2017 Rules introduced a 'wise use' principle allowing regulated activities — criticism of dilution
Wise use concept borrowed from Ramsar Convention — balancing conservation with sustainable use
UPSC trap: Distinguishing between prohibited activities (absolute ban) vs. regulated activities (permission-based)

concepts.name: Identification and Notification of Wetlands
key_dimensions: Process: States must prepare an inventory of wetlands and notify them — not automatic protection
Role of Space Applications Centre (SAC) and National Wetland Atlas in identification
UPSC trap: Notification by State government is required for protection — unnoted wetlands remain vulnerable
Comparison with Ramsar site designation which requires central government action and international notification

concepts.name: Ramsar Convention and Its Interface with 2017 Rules
key_dimensions: India is a Ramsar signatory (1982) — Ramsar sites get additional international recognition but domestic protection is under 2017 Rules
UPSC trap: Ramsar listing does not automatically confer legal protection under Indian law — 2017 Rules must apply
India has 75+ Ramsar sites (as of 2023) — highest in Asia; significance for Prelims
Montreux Record: Indian wetlands on it (Keoladeo, Loktak) — meaning of Montreux Record and its distinction from Ramsar listing

concepts.name: Role of MoEFCC vs. State Wetlands Authority: Division of Powers
key_dimensions: MoEFCC: nodal ministry, issues guidelines, coordinates Ramsar obligations, maintains national wetland inventory
State Wetlands Authority: actual regulatory power — grant/refuse permissions, prepare management plans
UPSC trap: MoEFCC does NOT directly regulate individual wetlands under 2017 Rules — States do
Concurrent List ambiguity: Environment is in Concurrent List — tension between state autonomy and national standards

concepts.name: Wetland Management Plans: Preparation and Implementation
key_dimensions: Mandatory for notified wetlands — prepared by State Wetlands Authority with community participation
Must be prepared within one year of notification — time-bound obligation
Contents: ecological character, threats, conservation measures, wise use provisions
UPSC trap: Management plans are required only for notified wetlands — not all identified wetlands

concepts.name: Role of District Collector and Local Bodies in Wetland Protection
key_dimensions: 2017 Rules explicitly include local bodies (Gram Panchayats, Urban Local Bodies) in governance — decentralization
District Collector has enforcement role for violations
Tension between development mandates of local bodies and conservation obligations
73rd/74th Amendment angle: Panchayati Raj institutions and environment management in Schedule XI/XII

concepts.name: Comparison: 2010 Rules vs. 2017 Rules — Key Differences
key_dimensions: Central Authority (2010) replaced by State Authorities (2017) — decentralization vs. dilution debate
2010 Rules: stricter prohibited activities, no regulated activities category; 2017 Rules: introduces 'regulated activities' — criticized as weakening protection
2017 Rules: include community/local body participation — improvement over 2010
UPSC high-yield: Parliamentary Standing Committee and environmentalists criticized 2017 Rules for reducing stringency

concepts.name: Wise Use Principle in Wetlands Conservation
key_dimensions: Derived from Ramsar Convention's 'wise use' concept: sustainable utilization compatible with ecosystem maintenance
First time formally incorporated in Indian wetland rules through 2017 Rules
UPSC trap: Wise use ≠ unrestricted use; it must maintain ecological character of the wetland
Examples: regulated ecotourism, traditional fishing rights, research activities as wise use

concepts.name: Buffer Zone Concept and Its Absence in 2017 Rules
key_dimensions: 2017 Rules do NOT mandate a specific buffer zone around wetlands — contrast with Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) or Eco-Sensitive Zones
States have discretion to define zones in management plans — criticized for lack of uniformity
UPSC trap: No fixed buffer distance prescribed unlike CRZ (500m) or ESZ provisions
Comparison: National Green Tribunal has in several orders directed buffer zones around specific wetlands despite absence in Rules

concepts.name: National Wetland Conservation Programme (NWCP) and its Relation to 2017 Rules
key_dimensions: NWCP is a financial/technical scheme by MoEFCC — separate from the regulatory 2017 Rules
Provides funds to States for conservation activities on identified wetlands
UPSC trap: NWCP predates 2017 Rules (started 1985-86) — Rules are regulatory, NWCP is programmatic
National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA) — later merged NWCP and river conservation — current status

concepts.name: Penalties and Enforcement Mechanism under 2017 Rules
key_dimensions: Penalties derived from parent Act (EPA 1986): imprisonment up to 5 years and/or fine up to ₹1 lakh
UPSC trap: 2017 Rules themselves do not specify fresh penalties — they invoke EPA 1986 penalties
Enforcement agencies: State Pollution Control Boards, District Collectors, State Wetlands Authorities
Criticism: weak enforcement, no dedicated wetland protection force, reliance on already-stretched SPCB machinery

concepts.name: Judicial Interventions in Wetland Protection: NGT and Supreme Court
key_dimensions: NGT has been more active than courts in wetland protection — suo motu cases on Yamuna floodplain, Pallikaranai marshland, Aarav Goel case
Supreme Court in M.C. Mehta cases and Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum established 'Precautionary Principle' applicable to wetlands
UPSC trap: NGT has jurisdiction over wetland violations under EPA 1986 (Schedule I of NGT Act 2010)
Judicial trend: Courts expanding 'Right to Environment' under Article 21 to protect wetlands from encroachment

concepts.name: Urban Wetlands: Special Challenges and Policy Gap
key_dimensions: Urban wetlands face dual pressure: real estate development + municipal waste dumping — not adequately addressed by 2017 Rules
National Wetland Inventory identified significant loss of urban wetlands (e.g., Bangalore lakes, Chennai's Pallikaranai)
Overlap with Master Plans under RERA, Town Planning Acts — conflict of laws issue
UPSC angle: Smart Cities Mission and urban wetland conservation — potential synergy vs. conflict

concepts.name: Ecological Services of Wetlands and Their Valuation
key_dimensions: Provisioning services (fish, water), regulating services (flood control, water purification), cultural services (tourism, heritage)
TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity) framework for wetland valuation — India's participation
UPSC trap: Carbon sequestration by wetlands (especially peatlands and mangroves) — blue carbon concept
Policy angle: Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES) mechanism not yet formally integrated into 2017 Rules

concepts.name: Mangroves and Coral Reefs: Special Status within Wetland Framework
key_dimensions: 2017 Rules include mangroves and coral reefs within 'wetland' definition — but they also have protection under CRZ Notification 2019
UPSC trap: Dual protection regime — CRZ 2019 (coastal wetlands/mangroves) AND Wetlands Rules 2017 — which prevails?
National Mangrove Committee under MoEFCC — separate advisory body
India's mangrove cover trend: increasing (per Forest Survey of India reports) — contrast with global decline
